groups.title: TypeScript's type system for Angular development
groups.question: A teammate passes a plain object into an Angular service that expects a Task interface, and it compiles. They also ask what @Component actually does. Explain both.

followUps.Structural typing and why shape matters: Why does a plain object satisfy an interface it was never declared as?
followUps.Decorators: how Angular uses them to att: What does a decorator like @Component do?

evidence.text: TypeScript checks whether a value has the required properties and types, not its declared name.
An object from anywhere that matches the shape is accepted.
This is why API response objects can be typed with interfaces without classes.

notEnough: Only saying TypeScript is structurally typed.

evidence.text: A decorator is a function applied to a class or member.
Angular's decorators attach metadata, such as a component's selector and template.
Angular reads that metadata to create and wire up the class.

groups.title: Classes and access modifiers in TypeScript
groups.question: You are writing an Angular service that injects HttpClient and returns typed task lists. Explain how access modifiers and generics help.

followUps.Public, private, protected, and readonly: Why mark injected dependencies private and some fields readonly?
followUps.Generics in TypeScript: type-safe reusab: What does the type parameter in http.get<Task[]>() give you?

evidence.text: private stops code outside the class from using a member.
readonly stops a value from being reassigned after construction.
These checks happen at compile time and do not exist in the output JavaScript.
Generics let one function work with many types.
The type parameter tells TypeScript what the response will contain.
You get typed results without casting, though the data is not checked at runtime.

notEnough: Only saying generics make code reusable.

groups.title: TypeScript tooling for an Angular project
groups.question: A new Angular project fails to compile with errors about possibly undefined values, and you need update and public versions of a User type. Explain the tsconfig settings and the utility types you would use.

followUps.tsconfig.json: strict, target, and Angul: What do strict, target and experimentalDecorators control in an Angular project?
followUps.Utility types: Partial, Required, Pick,: How would you build an update type and a public type from User?

evidence.text: strict turns on checks like catching possibly null or undefined values.
target sets which JavaScript version the compiler outputs.
Decorator settings let the compiler process Angular's decorators.

notEnough: Only saying tsconfig configures the compiler.

evidence.text: Partial makes every field optional, which suits update requests.
Omit removes fields like password and Pick keeps only chosen fields.
Record describes objects used as dictionaries.

groups.title: Enums, interfaces, and module organization
groups.question: Your app needs a Task shape from the API, a fixed set of task statuses, and an extra property added to a library's existing type. Explain how you would model each.

followUps.Interfaces for data shapes, enums for fi: When would you use an interface and when an enum?
followUps.TypeScript module augmentation and decla: How can you add a property to a type defined in a library without editing it?

evidence.text: Interfaces describe the shape of objects like API responses.
Enums or literal unions describe a fixed set of values like task statuses.
Interfaces vanish at runtime, while regular enums produce JavaScript objects.
Interfaces with the same name in the same scope merge their properties.
Module augmentation adds properties to a library's types from your own file.
This is how you add a user property to Express's Request type.

notEnough: Only saying you can extend interfaces.
